questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a defined chain of command matter more during a disaster than a routine incident?
options: The volume of stakeholders wanting information is much larger, and figuring out the chain of command live wastes time the recovery itself needs
SQL Server requires a chain of command to be configured before failover can occur
Routine incidents never need any communication structure at all
A chain of command is only relevant for Availability Groups, not other DR technologies
questions.explain: The larger scale of a disaster means improvising communication structure live costs more than during a smaller, routine incident.

questions.q: Why shouldn't the team doing the actual recovery work also field every stakeholder question, per this lesson?
options: Splitting attention between recovery and answering questions slows the technical work and produces rushed, worse answers to stakeholders
It's against SQL Server licensing terms
There's no real downside; it's simply traditional practice
The recovery team is not qualified to answer any questions
questions.explain: The lesson identifies this as a structural problem: both the technical work and the communication suffer when the same people do both under pressure.

questions.q: What is the structural fix for the recovery-team/communication overload problem, per this lesson?
options: A designated communication role, separate from the recovery team, that gets updates on a set cadence and translates them for stakeholders
Telling the recovery team to simply work faster and answer questions more efficiently
Eliminating all stakeholder communication during a disaster
Having every stakeholder communicate directly with the database server
questions.explain: The fix is structural — a dedicated role for communication, not asking the same people to do more of both jobs.

questions.q: What shape should a status update follow during a DR event, per this lesson (echoing SQL Server Database Administration's escalation lesson)?
options: Impact, current action, and an ETA only if it's genuinely known — honesty over false certainty
A precise ETA must always be given even if uncertain, to reassure stakeholders
Only technical jargon describing exact database internals
No status updates should be given until the incident is fully resolved
questions.explain: The lesson carries forward the same honest status-update shape, emphasizing that a wrong guessed ETA damages trust more than admitting uncertainty.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a guessed, wrong ETA during a disaster damage trust more than a similar mistake during a routine incident?
options: The audience and consequences are both larger at disaster scale — a wrong ETA might be repeated to leadership or customers, not just one internal team
Guessed ETAs are technically impossible to give during a disaster
There is no meaningful difference between the two situations
SQL Server logs and publicly displays every ETA given during an incident
questions.explain: Because more people, potentially including customers, are relying on the communicated ETA during a disaster, an inaccurate guess has a larger trust cost.
